16.1 · How Are Urban Areas Changing?

A Global Urban Transition

Urban areas are places where large numbers of people live together in relatively dense settlements and work nonagricultural jobs.

Tokyoholds more people than all of Earth did 6,000 years ago.
1800London became the first modern city past 1 million people.
2050urban populations are projected to double.
Why cities form: click one

Markets grow where goods change hands: ports, river crossings and crossroads.

Rail depots, highway junctions and airports pull in people and business.

Capitals gather government jobs, and the businesses that serve them.

Cities form around centers of trade, transportation, and political power, pulling people in through economic opportunity.

What cities replace: drag across

Urban development has transformed natural landscapes: more than 50% of Florida’s wetlands and more than 90% of California’s coastal wetlands have been altered or eliminated.

16.1 · Urban Ecology

The City as an Ecosystem

Urban ecology is the study of interactions between people and the urban environment.
Click a numbered circle (or a button) to see what urban ecologists study there.

1Habitat and species

Cities make new habitats. Some species thrive among people: coyotes in washes and parks, peregrine falcons nesting on towers, house finches at feeders. Others lose their habitat and disappear.

2The city’s metabolism

A city imports water, food, fuel, power and materials, and exports wastes: carbon dioxide, heat, sewage and trash. Urban ecologists trace these flows the way they would trace energy and nutrients through a forest.

3Heat and local climate

Pavement, roofs and walls soak up the day’s sun and release it at night, so the city stays warmer than the desert around it: the urban heat island.

4Water

Roofs and roads shed rain fast, carrying oil, metals and fertilizer into the river. A desert city also moves water in: canals carry it across the valley to taps, lawns and pools.

5People are part of it

Human choices shape the ecosystem. In metro Phoenix, wealthier neighborhoods have more plant diversity than poorer ones, a pattern ecologists call the luxury effect.

6Studying it for decades

Since 1997, ASU’s Central Arizona–Phoenix Long-Term Ecological Research program has studied the whole metro area as one ecosystem: people, plants, birds, soils, water and climate together.

Sources: Grimm et al., “Global change and the ecology of cities,” Science 319 (2008); Hope et al., “Socioeconomics drive urban plant diversity,” PNAS 100 (2003), the luxury effect in Phoenix; Central Arizona–Phoenix LTER (NSF and Arizona State University, since 1997).
16.1 · The Opportunity and Penalty of Urban Areas

Cities as Engines, and as Risks

The opportunity
GDP per person
New patents per person
Road surface per person
Serious crimes per person
  • Moving to a city twice the size yields about 15% higher income, thanks to denser networks of opportunity.
  • Economy of scale: per-capita costs for services fall as operations scale up, so a bigger city needs less road and pipe per person.
  • Shared resources (multi-unit buildings, transit) reduce per-capita energy and emissions.
The urban penalty
  • 19th-century industrialization created epidemics of cholera and other infectious diseases in crowded cities. In 1854, cholera killed 616 people around one water pump on Broad Street, London; John Snow mapped the deaths and traced them to the pump.
  • High pollution, a large ecological footprint and resource extraction grow with populations and economies; crime and disease also scale up with city size.
  • Developing cities still face many of these challenges, and the urban penalty persists in the Global South.
Sources: Bettencourt, Lobo, Helbing, Kühnert & West, “Growth, innovation, scaling, and the pace of life in cities,” PNAS 104 (2007): exponents 1.15 (GDP), 1.27 (new patents), 0.83 (road surface), 1.16 (serious crimes), measured per person relative to a city of 100,000. John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (1855); the map is a sketch after his, not a copy. Norton textbook.

16.1 · A Common Urban Challenge: Air Pollution

What Makes City Air Unhealthy?

Air Quality IndexFine particles (PM2.5)
64Moderate
Good
Moderate
Unhealthy for sensitive groups
Unhealthy
Very unhealthy
Hazardous

Ground-level ozone (smog)

Not emitted directly: nitrogen oxides from tailpipes and smokestacks react with vapors from fuel, paints and solvents in strong sunlight. It peaks on hot, sunny afternoons and inflames the lungs.

Fine particles (PM2.5)

Soot, dust and smoke smaller than a hair’s width, from engines, burning and construction. On calm winter nights an inversion traps them near the ground.

99% of the world’s people breathe air above WHO guideline levels; outdoor air pollution caused about 4.2 million early deaths in 2019. Metro Phoenix ranks among the ten most ozone-polluted U.S. metro areas.
Sources: U.S. EPA, AirNow “AQI Basics” and “Ground-level Ozone Basics”; WHO (2022), 99% of the world’s population; WHO fact sheet, Ambient (outdoor) air pollution (2024), 4.2 million deaths in 2019; American Lung Association, State of the Air (2024). The index values on this slide come from an illustrative model.
16.1 · The Urban Heat Island

Why Downtown Stays Hot

An urban heat island is a city area that is warmer than the rural areas around it.
Pavement, dark roofs and walls soak up the sun and give the heat back at night. Shade and evaporation from trees and plants, and roofs that reflect sunlight, cool the city.
Downtown vs. the countryside
+7.0°F

warmer at 4 pm

Phoenix, July 2023: 31 days in a row at or above 110°F. Maricopa County recorded 645 heat deaths that year.

Green roofs can be 30–40°F cooler than ordinary roofs; shaded surfaces can be 20–45°F cooler than sunlit ones.

Sources: U.S. EPA, “Learn About Heat Islands,” “Using Trees and Vegetation to Reduce Heat Islands” and “Using Green Roofs to Reduce Heat Islands”; National Weather Service Phoenix (31 straight days at 110°F or above, June 30 to July 30, 2023); Maricopa County Department of Public Health, 2023 Heat Deaths Report. The curve is an illustrative model scaled to EPA’s ranges.
16.3 · What Is Suburban Sprawl?

Suburban Sprawl: How It Happened

Suburban sprawl is the spread of urban populations away from city centers to widely dispersed, lower-density areas.

A compact streetcar town: shops, homes and the school within a short walk, surrounded by farms.

10 million new households formed 1945 to 1955. “Moving up” in class meant “moving out” of the city. FHA/VA loan guarantees, tax breaks and low interest rates made homeownership affordable, and large developers mass-produced homes from pre-cut kits.

The FHA and VA drew “red lines” around minority neighborhoods, denying them loans, and restrictive covenants barred ethnic groups from properties. In the 1920s, 95% of Los Angeles single-family homes were off-limits to Black and Asian people. Zoning separated people by race, class, and ethnicity.

The Federal-Aid Highway Act put $26 billion into 41,000+ miles of roads, making the suburbs easy to reach and older urban areas less attractive. The U.S. spent 8× more on roads than on mass transit.

Single-use zones and disconnected streets: sprawl consumes undeveloped land, reduces walking, increases miles traveled per capita, and worsens air quality. Baltimore city lost a third of its population from 1970 to 2010 while the Baltimore-DC metro area grew by two-thirds.

Both homes are the same distance from their school as the crow flies. On the grid you walk straight there; through the cul-de-sacs the streets loop you out to the arterial and around.

16.5 · What Is Urban Planning?

Planning Greener Places, at Every Scale

Green roofs can be 30–40°F cooler than ordinary roofs and can lower a city’s air temperature by up to 5°F. Bioswales and rain gardens soak up stormwater.

Seattle’s Bullitt Center exceeded the Living Building Challenge, the most ambitious green building standard, to become the world’s “greenest” commercial building.

The High Line is a public park built on an elevated rail line above Manhattan’s West Side: urban design that creates community in dense settings.

Freight trains stopped in 1980. In 1999 two neighbors founded Friends of the High Line to save it from demolition; the first section of the park opened in 2009. Participation matters: in Mumbai, residents’ own surveys of their settlements have shaped redevelopment plans.

Seoul’s Cheonggyecheon stream once ran in a concrete culvert under a road and an elevated expressway. In 2003 the city tore the expressway down; a 5.8 km (3.6 mile) stream park opened in 2005.

Air along the stream is 3.3 to 5.9°C (6 to 11°F) cooler than on a road a few blocks away. Fish species rose from 4 to 25 and birds from 6 to 36 (2003 to 2008).

The planner’s dilemma: commuters, rivers and smog cross city limits, so a region’s many local governments must agree on where to grow.

In 1979 Metro, the Portland area’s elected regional government (the only one in the U.S.), drew an urban growth boundary: build inside; keep farms and forests outside.

A full bus carries 70 passengers, but the average U.S. bus carries only 10. Streetcars average 46% of capacity and subways 24%. Mass transit works when density exists: many people living and working near the stops.

Sources: NACTO, Transit Street Design Guide (2016): people per hour a 10-foot lane can move at peak, normal operations (the designer uses each range’s midpoint); Norton textbook (transit loads).

Designing for people, not cars

Mixed-use areas

Housing, shops, restaurants, grocery stores, offices, and public amenities all within a half-mile of public transit, enabling walking and reducing car trips.

Transit-oriented development

Design strategies integrating public transportation and land-use patterns. Rail transit is most successful; bus rapid transit (dedicated lanes and signal priority) provides faster service at lower cost.

Walkability and pedestrian-oriented development

People walk more when protected from traffic, near interesting buildings, with trees and curbside parking as buffers. Some cities integrate bikes into pedestrian-oriented design.

Grid streets, not curvilinear loops

Short blocks with narrow streets in a grid give pedestrians a continuous, direct route between homes, shops, and schools. Curved cul-de-sacs and disconnected loops create long, indirect routes hostile to walking and cycling.

Induced traffic

Adding road lanes increases traffic and congestion, the opposite of the intended effect, because new capacity generates new demand.

16.6 · Transportation Shapes the Urban Landscape

How Transportation Shapes the City

Homes and shops grew within a short walk of the streetcar line.

The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 funded a 41,000-mile Interstate system. Streetcar rails came out; parking lots went in behind Main Street.

The average car sits parked about 95% of the time. In Los Angeles County, parking covers about 14% of incorporated land.

Parking lots become homes and plazas, with drop-off lanes on site. But a car that drops you off and circles until you return drives empty, adding traffic and emissions.

Rather than pay to park, an empty car could cruise slowly nearby, adding congestion.

One shared self-driving car could replace about 11 private cars, though with about 10% more miles driven.

Sources: Warner, Streetcar Suburbs (1962); Jackson, Crabgrass Frontier (1985); U.S. FHWA on the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956; Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking (2005); Chester et al., Journal of the American Planning Association (2015); Millard-Ball, “The autonomous vehicle parking problem,” Transport Policy (2019); Fagnant & Kockelman, Transportation Research Part C (2014). The drawing is illustrative.
